The Nature of Mass Demonstrations




John Berger




This article originally appeared in 

New Society

, 23 May 1968.




Seventy years ago (on 6 May 1898) there was a massive demonstration of workers, men and women, in the centre of Milan. The events which led up to it involve too long a history to treat with here. The demonstration was attacked and broken up by the army under the command of General Beccaris. At noon the cavalry charged the crowd: the unarmed workers tried to make barricades: martial law was declared and for three days the army fought against the unarmed.




The official casualty figures were 100 workers killed and 450 wounded. One policeman was killed accidentally by a soldier. There were no army casualties. (Two years later Umberto I was assassinated because after the massacre he publicly congratulated General Beccaris, the ‘butcher of Milan.’)




I have been trying to understand certain aspects of the demonstration in the Corso Venezia on 6 May because of a story I am writing. In the process I came to a few conclusions about demonstrations which may perhaps be more widely applicable.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The “enemy” isn’t in the streets. It’s what sends you there
content:
by Leonardo Caffo




from 

The Anarchist Library




From France to Albania, from Belgium to Turin, the protests of these days stage a clash between metaphors. Young people (the people) and police officers (the State), equally precarious, face each other as if the other were the enemy. But the enemy stopped living where we look for it long ago. And that is precisely where it organizes the anger, makes it visible and summons it into the street.




Let me say this right away, to leave no room for misunderstanding: the young people who have been filling the streets of Europe in recent weeks have every right to do so. This is not a rhetorical concession, one of those premises you write only to take back three lines later. They have reasons to spare: schools falling apart, overcrowded classrooms, a future shrinking like a room whose walls someone moves at night while we sleep. Anyone who dismisses them as vandals, as spoiled children of a prosperity they no longer know, or as puppets of some hidden director, has understood nothing. Or pretends not to understand, which is worse. But precisely because they are right, and precisely because their distress is real, it is worth asking the question nobody seems willing to ask these weeks. Not because it is difficult, but because it is uncomfortable for everyone: for governments, for movements, for newspapers, for commentators. The quest

author: Julius Gavroche
title: One, two … a thousand insurrections in France
content:

Tomás Ibáñez (18th of October 2026)




from

The intense events of 17 October, with their long list of violent clashes in many French cities, show that France could not be an exception. Just as has happened in recent years in many regions of the world – from the Americas to South-East Asia, via several European countries – we have witnessed on this occasion an outburst of discontent that had been slowly building up, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets and showing a determination capable of withstanding even the most forceful police crackdowns. As in so many other countries, the people who fuelled the demonstrations on this 17th of October did not do so by obeying slogans issued by large organisations, but primarily through social media, through everyday conversations circulating within the social fabric of neighbourhoods and workplaces, and also in response to calls from small organisations, without any centralising body acting as an intermediary between them.

content:
from the

A Report from Madrid and Barcelona




On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the 

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the 

Occupy

 movement in the United States.




Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.




Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.
